analysis.investment_thesis: Fujiyama is a genuine fast grower in India's solar boom — 39% revenue CAGR and 70% profit CAGR over 5 years — but at P/E 402 the PEG ratio is a shocking 5.7x, making this one of the most egregiously overpriced growth stories I've seen. The growth story is real; the price is fantasy.
key_strengths: Exceptional revenue momentum: 67% YoY jump to ₹1,539 Cr in FY25 with operating margins expanding to 17.2% from 9% in FY20
Sector tailwind is undeniable — India's rooftop solar push is visible everywhere, exactly the kind of story you can observe from street-level
ROE of 58% and operating profit CAGR of 53% show the business model is genuinely scaling with leverage
key_risks: PEG ratio of 5.7x (P/E 402 ÷ 70% earnings growth) — I don't pay more than 2x growth rate, and 5.7x is simply irrational
Severe earnings-cash disconnect: ₹156 Cr net profit but only ₹18 Cr OCF and -₹101 Cr FCF in FY25 — profits are not translating to real cash
Debt doubled to ₹395 Cr in FY25 while cash sits at just ₹8 Cr; D/E of 1.38 is well above my 0.6 comfort threshold
red_flags: OCF collapsed from ₹85 Cr (FY24) to ₹18 Cr (FY25) while net profit tripled to ₹156 Cr — this earnings quality gap demands scrutiny
Promoter holding of 86.76% means near-zero free float, making the stock susceptible to price manipulation and illiquidity
Finance costs rose 10x in 5 years (₹2 Cr → ₹22 Cr); debt-funded growth in a capital-intensive business is fragile
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Fujiyama ticks the fast-grower checklist on growth alone — 38.8% revenue CAGR, 70% profit CAGR, expanding margins — and the solar sector story is one you can verify just by driving through any Indian town. But the cardinal rule of GARP is that growth without a reasonable price is just speculation. At P/E 402 with a PEG of 5.7x, the stock is priced as if the next decade of growth is already baked in at peak multiples. I've never paid more than 2x the growth rate, and this asks for nearly 6x. That's not investing — that's gambling.

The cash flow picture is a serious warning sign beneath the headline profit surge. Net profit jumped to ₹156 Cr in FY25, but operating cash flow was only ₹18 Cr and free cash flow was -₹101 Cr. This divergence usually means aggressive receivables recognition or working capital traps common in EPC/project businesses. Meanwhile, debt doubled to ₹395 Cr against ₹8 Cr cash. The 86.76% promoter holding creates a thin float that can distort prices dramatically. This is a real business in a real tailwind sector — revisit if it ever trades near a PEG of 1.0 (implying a price around ₹45–55 on current earnings).
